books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Immigration figures: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States. Rounded figures.
stimulus.text:
| Decade | Immigrants arriving in the United States |
| 1831–1840 | about 600,000 |
| 1841–1850 | about 1.7 million |
| 1851–1860 | about 2.6 million |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The table best supports which conclusion about immigration before the Civil War?

options.text: Immigration fell sharply after 1840 and never recovered.
options.misconception: The table runs the other way: arrivals nearly triple from the 1830s to the 1840s, then rise again in the 1850s.

options.text: Immigration rose sharply in the 1840s and rose again in the 1850s.
Most immigrants in the 1850s came from Southern and Eastern Europe.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the 1850s wave came mainly from Ireland and Germany; Southern and Eastern Europe dominated a later wave, after 1890.
The 1850s row shows the largest arrivals of all, about 2.6 million; the flow grew, it did not stop.

rationales.A: The table runs the other way: arrivals nearly triple from the 1830s to the 1840s, then rise again in the 1850s.
rationales.B: From about 600,000 to 1.7 million to 2.6 million, each decade tops the last — a steep rise, not a fall.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the 1850s wave came mainly from Ireland and Germany; Southern and Eastern Europe dominated a later wave, after 1890.
rationales.D: The 1850s row shows the largest arrivals of all, about 2.6 million; the flow grew, it did not stop.
rationales.general:
1. Read the three rows in order: 600,000, then 1.7 million, then 2.6 million.
2. Compare each decade with the one before: every step is a large jump upward.
3. Name the pattern: a sharp rise across the 1840s and 1850s, not a decline, with each decade topping the last by a wide margin.
Remember: with a table, compare row to row before you reach for a cause.
